questions.question_text: The relationship between a qualifying broker and associate broker must be documented in:
distractors: A verbal understanding only
An NMREC-filed registration form
A notarized affidavit
questions.explanation: 16.61.16.9(J) NMAC requires the qualifying broker to execute and maintain written independent contractor agreements with affiliated brokers, while providing that no employer/employee relationship is required. The affiliation and its terms must be documented in a written agreement — verbal arrangements do not satisfy the rule (see also 16.61.17.8).

questions.question_text: For an associate broker to qualify as an independent contractor, which factor must be present?
questions.correct_answer: Compensation based on production, not hours
distractors: A minimum of 3 years experience
An office provided by the qualifying broker
A fixed monthly salary with bonuses
questions.explanation: IC status requires compensation tied to production (commissions), not hours worked. Other IC factors include a written agreement, broker not controlling work methods, and AB paying own taxes.

questions.question_text: A qualifying broker classifies an associate broker as an independent contractor but dictates their daily schedule and work methods. This arrangement:
questions.correct_answer: May not qualify as an IC relationship
distractors: Is standard IC practice in real estate
Is required by NMREC regulations
Only matters for tax filing purposes
questions.explanation: True IC status requires the broker not to control the means and methods of work. Dictating daily schedules contradicts IC criteria, regardless of what the written agreement says.

questions.question_text: An associate broker is classified as an independent contractor. The qualifying broker's supervisory obligation is:
questions.correct_answer: The same as for an employee AB
distractors: Reduced to periodic check-ins only
Limited to trust account oversight
Eliminated entirely for IC brokers
questions.explanation: Regardless of whether the AB is an employee or IC, the qualifying broker retains full supervisory responsibility and must ensure compliance with all laws and Commission rules.

questions.question_text: Who is responsible for paying income taxes on an associate broker classified as an independent contractor?
distractors: The qualifying broker's brokerage
NMREC deducts taxes from renewal fees
The state Regulation and Licensing Department
questions.explanation: One of the hallmarks of IC status is that the associate broker is responsible for their own taxes. The QB does not withhold taxes for independent contractor ABs.

questions.question_text: An associate broker publishes a full-length social media post marketing a listing, showing only her own name and cell number, with no link to anything. This post is:
questions.correct_answer: Prohibited because it omits the brokerage trade name and phone number
distractors: Compliant because social media posts are exempt from advertising rules
Compliant because posts under 200 characters never require disclosures
Compliant because consumers can reach the brokerage through her cell number
questions.explanation: Associate broker advertising must include the brokerage's trade name and current telephone number as registered with the commission (16.61.32.8(C) NMAC). Only limited displays of 200 characters or less — tweets, texts, thumbnails — may omit the disclosures, and only if linked to a display containing them (16.61.32.8(G)).

questions.question_text: A real estate team's yard sign shows the team name in large letters, with the brokerage trade name and phone number printed at one-tenth that size at the bottom. Is this sign compliant?
questions.correct_answer: No, the brokerage information must be at least one-third the type size of the team name
distractors: Yes, any size is acceptable as long as the brokerage name appears
No, team names may not appear on yard signs in New Mexico
Yes, if the sign also lists the team leader's license number
questions.explanation: The brokerage trade name and registered telephone number must be prominently displayed in a type size not less than thirty-three percent of the associate broker's or team's name (16.61.32.8(C) NMAC). Team names are permitted, but brokerage information at one-tenth the team-name size violates the floor.

questions.question_text: Under NMREC rules, what must an associate broker include when advertising real estate or real estate services?
questions.correct_answer: The brokerage trade name and phone number registered with the commission
distractors: The associate broker's license number
An NMREC advertising approval stamp
The brokerage's physical street address
questions.explanation: Associate broker advertising must include the brokerage's trade name and current telephone number as registered with the commission, at not less than thirty-three percent of the type size of the broker's or team's name (16.61.32.8(C) NMAC). License numbers, approval stamps, and street addresses are not required.

questions.question_text: A broker advertises a property as having "mountain views" when the view is actually of a parking lot. This advertising is:
questions.correct_answer: A violation of truthful advertising rules
distractors: Acceptable as marketing puffery
Permitted if the ad says views may vary
Allowed if the property has partial views
questions.explanation: All advertising must be truthful and not misleading. Claiming mountain views when the actual view is a parking lot is a clear misrepresentation.

questions.question_text: An associate broker's name appears on a billboard in type twice the size of the brokerage's registered trade name and telephone number. Under NMREC rules, this billboard is:
questions.correct_answer: Compliant, because the brokerage information is at least one-third the size of the associate broker's name
distractors: A violation, because the brokerage name must be at least as large as the associate broker's
A violation, because an associate broker's name may never dominate an ad
Compliant only if NMREC grants a written size waiver
questions.explanation: New Mexico sets a floor, not a ceiling: the brokerage trade name and telephone number must appear at not less than thirty-three percent of the type size of the associate broker's or team's name (16.61.32.8(C) NMAC). At half that size, the brokerage information complies.

questions.question_text: How long must a qualifying broker retain transaction records in New Mexico?
distractors: 3 years
5 years
10 years
questions.explanation: All trust and custodial account records and transaction records must be retained for 6 years after the completion of a transaction.

questions.question_text: Which documents must be included in a qualifying broker's transaction records?
distractors: Signed purchase contracts exclusively
Trust account bank statements only
Documents specifically requested by NMREC
questions.explanation: The qualifying broker must maintain all transaction records — listing agreements, purchase contracts, closing statements, and trust account receipt and disbursement records — for six years and make them available to the commission (16.61.16.9(F), 16.61.23.10, 16.61.23.11 NMAC). No single-document or on-request-only standard applies.

questions.question_text: A qualifying broker keeps all records in a cloud-based digital system. Under NM rules, this is:
questions.correct_answer: Acceptable if they meet Commission standards
distractors: Prohibited since paper records are mandatory
Allowed only for post-2020 transactions
Permitted only with prior NMREC approval
questions.explanation: Records may be kept in paper or electronic format (16.61.16.9(F) NMAC), so cloud storage is acceptable provided the records remain maintained at or accessible from the registered brokerage office and available to the commission for inspection (16.61.23.10(A) NMAC). No prior approval or paper-original rule exists.

questions.question_text: NMREC requests to inspect a brokerage's transaction records. How quickly must the qualifying broker provide access?
questions.correct_answer: Records must be readily accessible at all times
distractors: Within 30 business days of the request
Within 10 calendar days of written notice
At the next scheduled NMREC audit date
questions.explanation: Records must be maintained at or accessible from the registered brokerage office and be available to the commission or its authorized representative at the qualifying broker's place of business or the commission office (16.61.23.10(A), (D); 16.61.16.9(F) NMAC). The rules set no 10- or 30-day production window, so files must stay organized and producible.

questions.question_text: A transaction closed 5 years ago. The qualifying broker wants to destroy the records to save storage space. This would be:
questions.correct_answer: Premature because the 6-year period has not passed
distractors: Acceptable since transactions over 3 years old can be purged
Required to protect client privacy
Permitted because the transaction has closed and the file is final
questions.explanation: Transaction and trust account records must be retained for six years after completion of the transaction (16.61.16.9(F), 16.61.23.10(B) NMAC). Destroying the file at five years is a year early. Records may be kept electronically, but some complete form of the record must survive the full period.
